name: Architecture decision trees
description: Seven interactive decision trees for recurring architecture choices, each ending in a recommendation with trade-offs, watch-outs and when-not-to-pick conditions. ADR-shaped: usable as decision records.

decisions.title: Build or buy an AI gateway

q1.q: How many production GenAI use-cases will you run in the next 12 months?
q1.qhelp: An AI gateway centralises model routing, prompt/version pinning, evals hookup, guardrails, observability, cost attribution, and audit. The economics shift sharply around 2–3 use-cases; below that the buy/build question is mostly noise.

opts.label: One — we're shipping a single feature.
opts.body: Single chatbot, one assistant, one workflow. Maybe a second exploratory pilot.

leaf.title: Skip the gateway entirely. Use the provider SDK + a thin wrapper.
leaf.verdict: For one use-case, a gateway is over-engineering — you'll spend more time on plumbing than on the feature. Wrap the provider SDK in your own small llmClient module: one file, retry/timeout policy, hard-coded model+version, structured logging, eval-set-aware hook. When the second use-case lands, you re-run this decision.
when_to_pick: You're 6–12 weeks from shipping the only GenAI feature in the roadmap.
Your team has not yet defined a model-pinning policy or evals.
You're using one provider (OpenAI, Anthropic, Vertex, Bedrock) for everything.

pros: Lowest time-to-prod. Zero infrastructure to operate.
Easiest to migrate to a real gateway later (the wrapper becomes the interface).
No team-wide coordination tax.
cons: When the second use-case ships, you'll re-implement evals/logging/cost-attrib in two places.
Provider lock-in by default. Acceptable for one feature; painful at three.
No central place to enforce guardrails or audit policy.

watch_outs: Pin the model version explicitly. Avoid gpt-4o floating; use a dated alias. The hidden upgrade is the #1 cause of silent regressions.
Log prompt + retrieved context + model + version + output from day one. Replay is the only debugging tool you have.
Don't not evaluate just because you skipped the gateway. The eval-set is the gateway's job; without one, ship a CLI that runs 20 cases through your wrapper before each deploy.
leaf.when_not_to_pick: any use-case touches regulated decisions (clinical, credit, insurance, government benefits). At that point the audit + per-decision evidence pack obligation needs the gateway pattern even for one use-case.

opts.body: We're past the first feature, the org has greenlit two more in the next two quarters, and the team is starting to talk about "the GenAI platform."

opts.label: Six or more — this is now platform-shaped.
opts.body: We're funding a GenAI platform team. Multiple business lines have committed use-cases on the roadmap.

q2.q: Are you in a regulated industry (financial services, healthcare, government, critical infrastructure)?
q2.qhelp: Regulation shifts the threshold. EU AI Act high-risk obligations (2 Aug 2026 enforcement), APRA CPS 234, HIPAA audit trail, FDA SaMD post-market evidence — all need the per-decision audit pipeline that a gateway centralises.

opts.label: Yes — we're regulated.
opts.body: EU AI Act / APRA / HIPAA / SOCI / FDA. Audit + per-decision evidence is non-negotiable.

leaf.title: Buy a managed gateway and own the policy layer.
leaf.verdict: Buy the substrate (gateway + observability + provider abstraction); build the policy layer (prompt registry conventions, eval sets, guardrail rules, evidence-pack schema). Managed-gateway candidates: Portkey, LiteLLM (self-hosted but ops-light), AWS Bedrock + Guardrails, Azure AI Foundry, GCP Vertex AI. The build-vs-buy regret in regulated settings is one-way: building means you also re-implement evals, observability, and audit — usually badly — under audit-pressure deadlines.
when_to_pick: 2–5 GenAI use-cases on the roadmap.
EU AI Act high-risk classification likely (Annex III) for at least one use-case.
Your security/compliance team will need to attest to per-decision audit, not just usage logs.
You don't have a 5+ engineer GenAI platform team yet.

pros: Day-1 observability + guardrails + provider abstraction.
Vendor handles model-deprecation churn (provider model versions change quarterly).
Audit-friendly evidence pipelines are pre-built; you adapt rather than design.
Procurement vetted once; expansion to use-case 3, 4, 5 is config not code.
cons: Vendor risk: gateway is on the hot path of every LLM call.
Cost-per-call markup (varies; usually 0–15%). Negotiate.
Roadmap dependency. Their priorities aren't yours.
Data-residency / sovereignty: must verify (especially AU PROTECTED / EU sovereign requirements).

watch_outs: Validate the audit-pack output against your actual regulatory ask. Many gateways produce excellent observability and adequate (not regulatory-grade) audit evidence.
Test the failover path. Single-provider gateways become a single point of failure on top of the single point of failure they were supposed to mitigate.
Negotiate a data-processing agreement before signing. “Zero data retention” from the gateway vendor matters; from upstream providers also matters.
Keep your own prompt registry. The gateway is the proxy; the prompt + eval-set is your IP.
leaf.when_not_to_pick: you already have a 5+ engineer team specifically funded for the GenAI platform and a 3-year roadmap with sovereignty constraints that no commercial gateway can satisfy. In that case go to the 6+ use-case branch and consider building on top of LiteLLM or similar OSS.

q2a.q: Do you have, or are you funding, a GenAI platform team of 3+ engineers?
q2a.qhelp: A gateway is software; running one in production is operational work. Without a dedicated team, the operational tax is paid by whichever feature team is closest — usually the wrong one.

opts.label: Yes — 3+ dedicated engineers.
opts.body: We're treating GenAI as platform; we have headcount.

leaf.title: Buy the gateway. Build the policy & integration layer.
leaf.verdict: With a platform team, buy still wins on time-to-value, but the platform team's job is to own the integration shape: provider SDK abstraction, prompt registry, eval harness wired to CI, cost attribution, guardrail policy. Candidate gateways: Portkey, Helicone, LiteLLM (self-hosted), Bedrock + Guardrails, Azure AI Foundry. Re-evaluate at the 12 use-case threshold — that's the next natural decision point.
when_to_pick: 2–5 use-cases, multiple providers in play, internal platform-team funded.
Teams are starting to ask “which model are we on for X?”
Cost-per-feature is becoming an executive question.

pros: Fastest path from 2 to 5 use-cases.
Platform team adds value at the policy layer, not at the proxy plumbing layer.
Provider-swap is a config change, not an engineering project.
cons: Two layers to operate (gateway + platform-team integration).
Vendor markup on inference cost.
Migration risk if the chosen gateway gets acquired / sunsets.

watch_outs: Don't let the platform team build a custom gateway as a learning project. The opportunity cost is your second-quarter delivery.
Standardise on one prompt-registry tool (Langfuse, LangSmith, Promptfoo). The gateway logs calls; the registry holds the versioned prompts + evals. Two different tools.
Audit cost-attribution every month. Cost-per-token is the wrong unit; cost-per-resolved-task is the right one.
leaf.when_not_to_pick: your platform team is mainly a Kubernetes / observability team without ML/AI experience — they will struggle to evaluate evals + guardrails. Better to hire 1 ML-engineer first.

opts.body: GenAI work is distributed across feature teams; no central platform investment.

leaf.title: Buy the lowest-overhead managed gateway. Resist building.
leaf.verdict: Without a platform team, building a gateway is the surest way to discover that you needed a platform team. Pick the lowest-operational-overhead managed option (Portkey, Helicone, or your existing cloud's offering — Bedrock, Azure AI Foundry, Vertex AI) and let the feature teams consume a single endpoint with team-tagged API keys. Revisit at 6 use-cases or when one team starts maintaining their own bypass.
when_to_pick: 2–5 use-cases, no platform team, no clear path to one in the next two quarters.
Feature teams are starting to duplicate provider-handling code.
Finance has asked “what does each GenAI feature cost?”

pros: Cost attribution + observability + provider abstraction with near-zero ops.
Single procurement contract instead of 5.
Easy migration path when you do fund a platform team.
cons: Vendor markup; less control over edge cases.
Provider-team has roadmap power over you.
Without internal champion, the gateway becomes shelfware: teams route around when it inconveniences them.

watch_outs: Assign one named owner (even part-time) for the gateway across teams. The AI CoE Trap hits hardest here.
Don't pick a gateway that locks prompts inside its UI. Prompts live in git; gateway is the proxy.
leaf.when_not_to_pick: your security/compliance posture rules out third-party LLM-call inspection. Then self-host LiteLLM and accept the operational tax.

q3.q: Do you have hard data-residency / sovereignty constraints that no commercial gateway satisfies?
q3.qhelp: AU PROTECTED, EU sovereign-cloud-only, certain healthcare deployments — the gateway sits on the hot path of every prompt and response, so its hosting matters as much as the model's.

opts.label: Yes — sovereign / in-country only.
opts.body: Sovereign-cloud requirements rule out most commercial managed gateways.

leaf.title: Build on top of LiteLLM (or equivalent OSS). Operate it yourselves.
leaf.verdict: For 6+ use-cases under sovereignty constraints, the only viable shape is OSS-substrate-on-your-infrastructure. LiteLLM (Apache 2.0) gives you ~80% of a commercial gateway — provider abstraction, routing, retries, logging hooks, observability hooks — that you host in your VPC. You add: prompt registry (Langfuse self-hosted), eval harness, audit pipeline, internal cost-attribution. Plan for 1.5–3 FTE on the gateway+integration layer steady-state. Treat this as platform investment, not project work.
when_to_pick: 6+ use-cases under sovereignty constraints commercial gateways can't satisfy.
You have a 5+ engineer platform team with at least 1 ML-experienced engineer.
Provider model-choice flexibility is strategic (you want to be able to swap Anthropic ↔ OpenAI ↔ open-weights).

pros: Full control over data path, audit, eval, guardrail logic.
No vendor markup on per-call cost.
Sovereignty-compliance is yours to attest, not your vendor's.
cons: Operational tax: 1.5–3 FTE steady-state, more during incidents.
Provider-version churn lands on your team (model deprecations, API changes).
Internal-tools UX always lags commercial gateways; teams will complain.

watch_outs: Don't fork the OSS unless absolutely necessary. Upstream-tracking is the #1 maintenance burden.
Wire eval-gated CI from day one. The minute prompts are not versioned-with-evals, the platform's value disappears.
Plan the migration from your own gateway to a commercial one as a fallback option. Treating it as “forever” lets bad designs entrench.
leaf.when_not_to_pick: your platform team is <5 engineers or doesn't have ML experience — you'll under-deliver and the experience will sour the org on platform work generally.

pros: Lowest aggregate operational cost across 6+ use-cases.
Provider abstraction + observability + cost attribution out of the box.
Procurement + DPA done once; scale-out is config.
cons: Vendor on hot path. Acceptable if SLA is real; review monthly.
Markup on per-call cost; negotiate volume tiers.
Custom audit needs (per-decision evidence shape) are your team's work, not the vendor's.

watch_outs: Run a 90-day pilot with two providers before signing a multi-year deal.
Cap gateway-vendor data retention to zero by contract.
Confirm region-pinning of inference; some gateways route across regions for capacity and that breaks AU/EU data-residency claims.
leaf.when_not_to_pick: your cost-per-token is your headline business metric (e.g. you're shipping inference at consumer-app scale) — the markup at that volume is the build justification.

q1.q: Does your use-case depend primarily on knowledge or on behaviour?
q1.qhelp: The single most common mistake in LLM-product design is reaching for fine-tuning when the problem is knowledge (use RAG), or reaching for RAG when the problem is behaviour (use fine-tuning or prompt design). The two problems look similar; the right shape is opposite.

opts.label: Knowledge — answers depend on specific facts/docs the base model doesn't know.
opts.body: Customer-support over your KB. Q&A over your codebase / specs / policies. Compliance-aware answering. Internal-doc search.

opts.label: Behaviour — the model must respond in a specific style/format/decision-shape.
opts.body: Always-JSON output. Specific tone. Decision rules learned from many examples. Classification with domain-specific labels.

opts.label: Both — need new knowledge AND new behaviour.
opts.body: E.g. customer-support that uses your KB AND follows a strict response format AND escalates on specific triggers.

q2_kn.q: How often does the knowledge change?
q2_kn.qhelp: Knowledge that changes weekly/daily must be retrievable; knowledge that's stable for years can be a candidate for fine-tuning. The threshold isn't strict, but the further you move from “changes daily” the more options open up.

opts.label: Often — docs change weekly or faster.
opts.body: Product docs, policy updates, ticket history, code changes.

leaf.title: RAG. The right primitive for changing knowledge.
leaf.verdict: For changing knowledge, RAG is the right pattern. Retrieve relevant context at query-time, pass it to the model, ground the answer in it. Cite the source. The model stays general; the knowledge stays current; the failure modes are debuggable (you can see which docs were retrieved). Fine-tuning for this use-case is anti-pattern: every doc update means a retrain.
when_to_pick: Knowledge changes faster than your training cadence.
Citations / source-attribution is a requirement.
You need to add/remove docs without redeploying the model.

pros: Knowledge updates are data ops, not training ops.
Citations + provenance are natural.
Failure mode ("retrieved the wrong context") is debuggable.
cons: Retrieval quality is the bottleneck; bad retrieval = bad answers.
Latency: retrieval + LLM call instead of just LLM call.
Cost: longer prompts (retrieved context tokens).

watch_outs: Chunking strategy matters more than embedding choice. Test 200/500/1000-token chunks with overlap; tune before optimising the embedding model.
Hybrid search (BM25 + vector) beats vector-alone in most enterprise corpora. Read Anthropic's contextual retrieval post.
Treat the eval set as part of the RAG system: 50 known-answer cases, run on every prompt or retriever change.
Show citations to the user. Forces the system to be honest about what it retrieved.
leaf.when_not_to_pick: your knowledge is stable and the failure mode is behaviour, not facts (a customer-service tone that needs many examples). Use fine-tuning.

opts.label: Rarely — the knowledge is stable for years.
opts.body: E.g. domain ontology, slow-moving regulatory text, well-defined product taxonomy.

leaf.title: RAG first; consider fine-tune only if retrieval fundamentally underperforms.
leaf.verdict: Even for stable knowledge, RAG is the right default — the source-of-truth stays in the docs, citations work, debugging is straightforward. Only consider fine-tuning if you've proven RAG hits a quality ceiling: the model needs to internalise a vocabulary or ontology to reason fluently in it, and prompt-stuffed examples aren't enough. Even then, fine-tune on top of RAG (RAFT-style approaches), don't replace it.
when_to_pick: Stable knowledge, RAG-first delivery, prove it before considering FT.
Citations / provenance are still a requirement.
You haven't yet hit a quality ceiling you can attribute to retrieval failure.

pros: Same as the high-change case — updates are data ops.
Optionality: you can fine-tune later if proven necessary.
Simplest path to first defensible answer.
cons: Some queries that would benefit from learned vocabulary still pay the retrieval-quality tax.

watch_outs: Don't fine-tune as the first move. Fine-tune-without-RAG is the most common expensive mistake.
If you eventually fine-tune, fine-tune on top of RAG (RAFT-style). The model learns to use retrieved context better; it doesn't replace it.
leaf.when_not_to_pick: the use-case is genuinely behavioural (output format / decision style) rather than knowledge-driven. Go to the behaviour branch.

q2_bh.q: How many examples of the desired behaviour can you reliably curate?
q2_bh.qhelp: Fine-tuning needs data. Below ~50 high-quality examples, prompt engineering beats fine-tuning; above ~1000, fine-tuning starts to win on consistency + cost. The middle is judgement-and-eval-set territory.

opts.label: Fewer than ~50 good examples.
opts.body: Small dataset, hand-curated, hard to grow without manual labelling effort.

leaf.title: Prompt engineering + few-shot examples. Fine-tuning is not justified.
leaf.verdict: Below ~50 examples, prompt engineering with few-shot examples beats fine-tuning on cost, latency, and iteration speed. Use the examples as in-context demonstrations; pin the model version; build an eval set from the same examples (split train/eval to avoid overfit). Re-evaluate fine-tuning when you have 200+ examples or the prompt becomes unwieldy.
when_to_pick: Small dataset of desired-behaviour examples.
Iteration speed matters more than absolute accuracy.
You haven't established a defensible eval set yet.

pros: Cheapest, fastest, most reversible.
Prompt + few-shot is iterable in minutes; fine-tunes take hours.
No model-lifecycle to manage.
cons: Token cost per call is higher (examples in every prompt).
Consistency varies more than fine-tuned models.
Prompt-length ceiling caps the number of examples you can pass.

watch_outs: Don't skip the eval set even at this scale. 20 cases is enough to catch the bad changes.
Pin model version explicitly. Prompt-engineered behaviour can drift across silent model updates.
Capture all production prompts in the registry — not in inline code (Inline Prompt Pattern).
leaf.when_not_to_pick: consistency is the hard requirement (e.g. always-valid-JSON, always-same-format) and even with few-shot you're seeing >5% format violations. Then fine-tune or use a constrained-decoding library.

opts.label: 50–1000 examples.
opts.body: Solid dataset, not enormous. Curated from production traffic or domain experts.

leaf.title: Try both. Fine-tune a small model as the production-quality target; keep prompted larger model as the backstop.
leaf.verdict: In this band, the answer is empirical: fine-tune a small model (e.g. Llama 3 8B / GPT-4o-mini / Claude Haiku) and benchmark against a prompted larger model on your eval set. Often the fine-tuned small model wins on cost-per-task and consistency; the prompted large model wins on edge-case robustness. Production shape: fine-tuned model as the default path, large model as fallback when confidence is low.
when_to_pick: 50–1000 high-quality examples.
Cost-per-call is meaningful at your volume.
Consistency on the happy-path matters.

pros: Cost reduction often 5–20x vs always-large-model.
Consistency improves (the model learns the format).
Backstop pattern (fine-tune for routine, large for edge) handles both.
cons: Two models to maintain (fine-tuned + fallback).
Fine-tune cycle adds CI/CD complexity.
Drift: production distribution shifts, fine-tuned model needs refresh.

watch_outs: Hold-out evaluation: never evaluate on training examples. The split is the first thing reviewers ask about.
Monitor production distribution shift. The fine-tuned model's accuracy decays as the real distribution diverges from your training set; plan refresh cadence.
Don't fine-tune a closed-weights model lightly. Vendor lock-in deepens; portability vanishes.
leaf.when_not_to_pick: your volume is low and the cost-per-call savings don't justify the additional pipeline. Stay on prompted-large-model.

opts.label: More than ~1000 examples.
opts.body: Large dataset, growing organically from production.

leaf.title: Fine-tune a small model as the production default.
leaf.verdict: Above ~1000 examples, fine-tuning a small model (or LoRA-tuning) is the cost-and-consistency winner for behaviour-shaped tasks. Use the prompted large model only as a fallback for low-confidence cases. Pipeline: training data → fine-tune → eval-gate (must beat baseline on hold-out) → deploy as default → measure production accuracy + cost. Plan retrain cadence quarterly (or distribution-shift-triggered).
when_to_pick: 1000+ high-quality examples, growing.
Cost-per-call is a material business metric.
You have ML / data-engineering capability on the team.

pros: Best cost-per-call.
Best consistency on training distribution.
Smaller models inference faster (latency win).
cons: Training pipeline is real engineering work.
Distribution drift management is ongoing.
Open-weights model picks bring infra responsibility.

watch_outs: Treat the training data as the most valuable artefact. Version it; review additions; gate eval-set changes.
Eval-set must beat the prompted baseline by a meaningful margin before deploy. Marginal wins don't justify the pipeline cost.
Plan a fallback path to the prompted model for production incidents (bad training run, distribution shift).
leaf.when_not_to_pick: you don't yet have an eval set that the team trusts. Build the eval discipline first; fine-tune second.

q2_both.q: Is the behaviour requirement strict (e.g. always-JSON, always-cite, always-escalate-on-X)?
q2_both.qhelp: When you need both new knowledge AND new behaviour, the question is whether the behaviour is loose (style/tone) or strict (format/decision rule). Strict behaviour calls for a different ground-truthing approach.

opts.label: Strict — format / decision rules / escalation triggers must be exact.
opts.body: Always-valid-JSON; always-cite-source; escalate-on-trigger-X; deny-list-on-Y.

leaf.title: RAG + guardrails + (optionally) fine-tuned router. Don't fine-tune the answering model.
leaf.verdict: When knowledge and strict behaviour both matter, the right shape is: RAG for knowledge + layered guardrails for strict behaviour + (optionally) a fine-tuned small “router” model for routing/escalation decisions. The answering model stays a general LLM with RAG context; the strict-behaviour requirements are enforced by guardrails (output schema validation, classifier-based content checks, structured-output decoding) and the routing decisions (escalate? deny? clarify?) are a separate small fine-tuned classifier. This is what most regulated-industry GenAI systems actually look like in production.
when_to_pick: Need new knowledge AND strict format/decision behaviour.
Regulated or high-stakes domain (clinical, financial, government).
Audit obligation for both the knowledge basis and the decision shape.

pros: Separation of concerns: each component is debuggable.
Routing decisions are deterministic (small classifier or rules), not LLM-magic.
Auditable end-to-end: retrieved context + applied guardrails + routing decision.
cons: More moving parts than pure prompt-RAG.
Routing model needs its own training + eval.
Latency: retrieval + LLM + guardrail + router.

watch_outs: Don't try to encode the strict behaviour in the prompt alone. Prompts drift; guardrails don't.
Use a structured-output library (Pydantic + instructor / outlines / DSPy) instead of begging the LLM for JSON.
Test adversarial cases against the guardrail layer. The behaviour requirements are the threat model.
leaf.when_not_to_pick: knowledge isn't actually changing — you might be over-engineering. Re-check whether knowledge is truly dynamic or whether it could live in a prompt.

opts.label: Loose — style / tone / general format.
opts.body: Want a specific brand voice or general response shape; small deviations are OK.

leaf.title: RAG + a behaviour-aware system prompt. Iterate; consider fine-tune later if needed.
leaf.verdict: For knowledge + loose behaviour, RAG plus a system prompt that encodes the tone/format + 2–5 in-context examples is usually enough. Don't over-engineer. If after a quarter the behaviour still drifts (drift = the system prompt is too long, edge cases keep slipping), then fine-tune a small model on a curated set of behaviour examples while keeping RAG as the knowledge source.
when_to_pick: Knowledge + style/tone but no strict format/decision rules.
You're early in the use-case lifecycle; iteration matters.
Low-to-medium-stakes domain.

pros: Lowest engineering investment.
Iterable in days, not months.
Easy migration path to fine-tune if needed later.
cons: Consistency on tone/format is in the 80–95% range, not 99%+.
Token cost slightly higher (system prompt + examples in every call).

watch_outs: Eval-set covers tone/format checks too, not just answer correctness.
If the system prompt grows past ~2000 tokens, you're past the “loose behaviour” threshold — revisit the strict-behaviour branch.
leaf.when_not_to_pick: the use-case is regulated or has any strict-output requirement — go strict-behaviour.

q1.q: Where will policy decisions need to be evaluated?
q1.qhelp: Policy-as-code is the encoded form of architecture principles. The right engine depends almost entirely on where the decision needs to be made — the policy language is secondary. The three serious options today are OPA (general-purpose, Rego language), Kyverno (Kubernetes-native, YAML/CEL), and Cedar (AWS-originated, fine-grained authorisation).

opts.label: Kubernetes admission — that's it.
opts.body: Block bad manifests at deploy. No CI/CD policy. No app-level authorisation. Just admission control on the cluster.

leaf.title: Kyverno. Kubernetes-native; the lowest-friction win.
leaf.verdict: Kyverno is the right answer for “just Kubernetes admission”. Policies are YAML (the language your team already speaks), the CRDs match Kubernetes conventions, mutation + validation + image-verification + generation all in one engine. No Rego learning curve, no sidecar to operate. CNCF Graduated — production-grade.
when_to_pick: Your policy surface is “deploys that violate X should fail” on a Kubernetes platform.
Team is YAML-native; Rego learning would slow the win.
You want image-signature verification (cosign) in the same engine.
Multi-tenant clusters where namespace-scoped policy varies.

pros: Lowest time-to-first-enforced-rule of any option.
Mutation + validation + image-verify + generation in one tool.
Strong defaults: the policy library at kyverno.io/policies covers 80% of common admission rules.
CNCF Graduated; stable production base.
cons: Kubernetes-only. Will not help you with CI/CD, IaC, or app-authz.
YAML logic grows ugly fast for complex rules; reach for CEL when YAML gets unwieldy.
If you adopt OPA later for something else, you'll have two engines.

watch_outs: Run new policies in audit mode first. Move to enforce after a sprint of clean reports.
Wire policy reports to a backstop dashboard. Without visibility, even audit-mode failures get ignored.
Don't try to enforce business rules at admission. Admission is for invariants (signed images, ownership annotations); business logic belongs in app/CI policy.
leaf.when_not_to_pick: you also need to enforce policy in CI (Terraform-plan-time, container-build-time) or at runtime in applications. You'll either run two engines or wish you'd picked OPA.

opts.label: Multiple surfaces — admission + CI + IaC + maybe app.
opts.body: We want one engine for K8s admission, Terraform plan validation (conftest), CI image checks, and possibly per-API authz.

opts.label: Per-resource app authorisation — that's the main job.
opts.body: We need fine-grained, per-resource authorisation in services (e.g. "can user X read document Y in role R"). Often paired with RBAC + ReBAC + ABAC patterns.

q2.q: Do you have, or are you ready to invest in, Rego skill on the team?
q2.qhelp: OPA + Rego is the multi-surface answer — admission (via Gatekeeper or OPA), CI (via conftest), IaC plan-time, application-authz (via OPA sidecar or library). Rego is genuinely different from imperative code; teams that don't invest land in a worse place than not having policy-as-code at all.

opts.label: Yes — we'll learn Rego.
opts.body: Team has appetite for a new DSL, or already has Rego experience. CNCF/security skills present.

leaf.title: OPA. One engine across admission, CI, IaC, and (optionally) app authz.
leaf.verdict: OPA is the multi-surface answer. One engine, one language (Rego), one bundle-distribution mechanism. Run it at K8s admission (via Gatekeeper or OPA-as-admission), at CI plan-time (conftest for Terraform/JSON/YAML), at container-build time (conftest on Dockerfiles), and optionally as a sidecar for application authorisation. CNCF Graduated. The trade-off is Rego itself — budget 2–4 weeks for the team to get past “why does this look like Prolog” to fluent.
when_to_pick: Policy surface spans 3+ enforcement points (admission, CI, IaC, app).
Team will invest in Rego (and you have or can hire one champion).
You want a single audit story: one engine's logs, one rules repo, one CI pipeline.

pros: Genuinely general-purpose; one engine reduces the cognitive-load tax.
Excellent test framework (Rego unit tests in CI).
Bundle-server pattern lets you version + roll out policy changes cleanly.
Mature OSS (graduated CNCF), strong ecosystem, big-co usage.
cons: Rego learning curve is real; without a champion the rollout stalls.
Operational surface is larger than Kyverno (especially Gatekeeper).
For K8s-only use-cases, Kyverno is faster to value.

watch_outs: Pick one champion who owns Rego conventions. Without a style/test convention, the rules repo becomes the next PDF (unreadable by anyone but the author).
Treat policy bundles like application releases. Versioned, staged (audit → enforce), reversible.
Mind admission performance. Heavy ConstraintTemplate queries on Gatekeeper can slow the API server. Profile before rolling out org-wide.
leaf.when_not_to_pick: your team's bandwidth is already saturated and you only need K8s admission today. The Rego cost isn't worth it for one surface.

opts.label: No — we won't invest in Rego.
opts.body: Team is small or stretched; learning a DSL would derail the rollout.

leaf.title: Kyverno for K8s. Checkov + tflint for IaC. Accept the two-engine tax.
leaf.verdict: Without Rego investment, the right multi-surface answer is “the best tool per surface, accept the heterogeneity.” Kyverno for Kubernetes admission, Checkov + tflint for Terraform / CloudFormation / Kubernetes-IaC at plan-time, native cloud-provider policy (AWS SCPs, Azure Policy, GCP Org Policy) for cloud control. Two-or-three engines, but each in a language the team already reads. Re-visit when team has bandwidth to evaluate OPA again.
when_to_pick: Multi-surface need but team can't absorb a DSL right now.
Cloud-native posture leans into provider-native policy (AWS SCPs / Azure Policy).
You want short time-to-first-enforced-rule above engine-consolidation.

pros: Each tool is approachable in its native form.
Cloud-provider policy gives you a guardrail before workloads even reach a cluster.
Lower training cost than OPA in the short term.
cons: Audit story has multiple sources; consolidating into one report needs effort.
Policy duplication risk: the same intent encoded in two engines drifts.
Decision-fatigue: every new surface needs a new policy-engine evaluation.

watch_outs: Maintain a single policy catalogue (markdown / docs). Each policy file lists which engine enforces it and where, so the duplication is visible.
Re-evaluate quarterly. Tool-sprawl is fine while it's tracked and shrinking; bad when it's invisible and growing.
leaf.when_not_to_pick: you're being audited against a single regulatory framework (e.g. CPS 234) that expects one consolidated policy attestation — the multi-engine evidence trail will become work later.

q3.q: Is the authz model fixed-RBAC, or does it need fine-grained ReBAC / ABAC with policy-language flexibility?
q3.qhelp: Application-level authorisation has its own engine landscape: AWS Cedar (and the Cedar-derived Verified Permissions service), OpenFGA (Google Zanzibar-inspired ReBAC), SpiceDB (also Zanzibar-style), and OPA-as-sidecar. The choice splits on whether the model is closer to roles or relationships.

opts.label: RBAC + attribute checks — roles plus a few attributes.
opts.body: Per-resource roles, plus attribute-based rules (department = X, region = Y, classification = Z).

leaf.title: Cedar (or AWS Verified Permissions if you're on AWS).
leaf.verdict: Cedar is the right fit for RBAC + ABAC at the application layer. The language is purpose-built for authz (much easier to read than Rego), the model maps cleanly to typical SaaS / enterprise-app authz needs, and AWS Verified Permissions gives you a managed Cedar evaluation service if you're on AWS. Open-source under Apache 2.0; rust-based reference implementation; bindings for major languages.
when_to_pick: App-level per-resource authz with roles + attributes.
You want a language designed for authz (not a general policy DSL).
On AWS, Verified Permissions removes most operational concerns.

pros: Authz-purpose-built language: smaller learning curve than Rego for authz use-cases.
Formal analysis: Cedar policies have provable properties (which Rego does not).
AWS Verified Permissions is a credible managed option.
cons: Newer ecosystem (compared to OPA); fewer war stories.
Not designed for K8s admission or CI policy — authz only.
If you're multi-cloud and want the same engine everywhere, Verified Permissions doesn't help.

watch_outs: Model the entity store before writing policies. Cedar's strength is the entity model; design that first.
Treat policies as a versioned artefact, not a config table. Authz changes are deployments.
leaf.when_not_to_pick: your authorisation model is heavily relationship-based (Google Docs / Notion / Linear style "who can access what through which sharing chain"). Use OpenFGA or SpiceDB instead.

next_steps.title: Cedar policy language docs
next_steps.body: Read the spec and run the examples before committing.

opts.label: ReBAC — relationships drive permissions.
opts.body: Permissions flow through relationships: folders contain documents, teams contain users, share-links grant access. Google Docs / Notion / Linear-shaped authz.

leaf.title: OpenFGA (or SpiceDB). Zanzibar-style ReBAC.
leaf.verdict: OpenFGA is the OSS Zanzibar-inspired ReBAC engine for relationship-driven authz (CNCF Sandbox; backed by Auth0/Okta). SpiceDB (AuthZed) is the equivalent commercial-friendly option. Both implement the Google Zanzibar paper that powers Drive / Docs / YouTube / Calendar authz. Pick OpenFGA for OSS + community; SpiceDB for managed cloud + commercial support.
when_to_pick: Permissions flow through relationships, not just role assignments.
“Can user U do action A on resource R?” is the question millions of times per second.
Per-resource sharing (links, invites, nested folders) is core to the product.

pros: Purpose-built for ReBAC at scale.
Latency-optimised consistency model (zookies / consistency tokens).
Strong eventing model for permission changes.
cons: Model design is the hard part; teams underestimate it.
Operational footprint is non-trivial (datastore + service).
Migration from a roles-table to ReBAC is a meaningful project.

watch_outs: Read the Zanzibar paper. The model is not intuitive without it.
Don't model business logic in the authz schema. ReBAC is for “can”; business rules go in the service.
Plan for the migration path from your current authz table to ReBAC. It's typically 2–4 quarters of work for a real product.
leaf.when_not_to_pick: your authz is fundamentally RBAC + simple attributes — you'll over-engineer with ReBAC and pay the operational + cognitive tax for years.

q1.q: Will any one customer's load, blast-radius, or compliance need to exceed the others by >10x?
q1.qhelp: Tenancy determines blast-radius, cost shape, deployment cadence, and audit story. The three credible models are: shared multi-tenant (one app, all customers, namespaces or tenant IDs in the data model), cell-based (sharded into independent “cells” with N customers per cell), and single-tenant (one stack per customer). Pick the wrong one and you'll re-platform mid-growth.

opts.label: No — customer load and posture is uniform.
opts.body: Customers are similar in size, regulation, and SLA. Internal benchmark: top-10% is <5x median.

opts.label: Yes — we have one (or will have) a 10x+ customer.
opts.body: Big enterprise contract, public-sector tenant with sovereignty requirements, or one customer driving 50%+ of traffic.

opts.label: Yes — many tenants are heterogeneous (mix of small + big).
opts.body: Long-tail of small tenants plus a chunky head of enterprise tenants with distinct SLA / data-residency / version needs.

q2.q: Are you under hard data-isolation constraints (per-tenant encryption keys, sovereign data residency, regulator-required dedicated storage)?
q2.qhelp: Even uniform-load workloads sometimes face hard isolation rules — healthcare PHI, government PROTECTED data, certain financial-services regulators. These are gates the architecture must respect.

opts.label: No — logical isolation is acceptable.
opts.body: Standard SaaS-grade isolation: per-tenant IDs in the data model, IAM / RLS guards, encrypted at rest with a shared key.

leaf.title: Shared multi-tenant. Highest leverage; most operational simplicity.
leaf.verdict: Shared multi-tenant is the right shape for uniform-load, soft-isolation SaaS. One application; one data plane; tenant ID propagated through every query (RLS in Postgres, or app-layer guards). Lowest unit cost; fastest feature rollout; easiest to operate. Discipline matters more than tooling here: tenant-ID propagation must be 100% covered by tests; cross-tenant data leaks are the failure mode and they're often discovered by a customer, not by you.
when_to_pick: Uniform load + soft isolation + you have a small platform team.
Per-tenant cost is going to be low (consumer-SaaS or low-ARPU B2B).
Feature-rollout velocity is your competitive advantage.

pros: Lowest unit cost. Resources are shared; idle capacity amortises.
Single deployment pipeline; features land for everyone at once.
Smallest operational footprint.
cons: Blast-radius is global: a P0 bug affects every customer.
Noisy-neighbour risk: one tenant's burst affects others.
Per-tenant configurability is limited; one-off requirements compound.

watch_outs: Enforce tenant-ID at the data layer (RLS in Postgres, query-guard middleware in Mongo/DynamoDB). Application-layer-only enforcement always eventually fails.
Write a tenant-isolation test that runs in CI. Asserts no query path bypasses tenant scoping. This is the single highest-ROI test you can write.
Plan the migration to cell-based now, even if you don't ship it. Your data model should already include a logical “cell ID” field so the sharding move later is non-breaking.
leaf.when_not_to_pick: any tenant brings dedicated-storage or per-tenant-KMS requirements. At that point you're forcing the architecture to do work it wasn't designed for.

next_steps.title: SRE Programme
next_steps.body: Blast-radius and noisy-neighbour are SRE concerns; this surfaces where you stand.

opts.label: Yes — hard isolation required.
opts.body: Per-tenant KMS keys, dedicated storage volumes per regulated tenant, sovereign-residency-per-tenant.

leaf.title: Cell-based — one cell per isolation-class. Don't go fully single-tenant unless forced.
leaf.verdict: Hard-isolation requirements push you to cell-based architecture: each cell is a self-contained slice of the app + data, and tenants are placed into cells based on isolation class (e.g. one cell per sovereign region; one cell for hard-isolated tenants; the rest sharded across general cells). The pattern from AWS Builder's Library on cell-based architecture is canonical. Single-tenant only when the customer contractually demands it and pays for the dedicated stack — otherwise the operational tax is brutal.
when_to_pick: Hard isolation needed for some tenants, but you still want operational economies of scale.
Sovereign-residency varies by tenant.
You have a platform team that can operate fleet-of-cells (Terraform + control plane for placement).

pros: Per-cell blast-radius: P0 in one cell doesn't affect others.
Per-cell rollout: progressive deployment is natural.
Per-cell scaling: noisy-neighbour stays inside one cell.
Tenant-placement engine is your isolation-policy lever.
cons: Significant control-plane work: routing, placement, fleet management.
Multi-cell observability is harder than single-stack.
Schema migrations across many cells need coordination + tooling.
Per-cell idle cost adds up.

watch_outs: Build the control plane before you need it. Cell placement, tenant routing, fleet config — bolting on later is painful.
Treat cells as cattle. Per-cell snowflakes erase the model's benefits.
Plan schema-migration tooling. Migrating N cells safely is a tooling problem, not a heroics problem.
leaf.when_not_to_pick: you're a 3-engineer team running a SaaS with 50 customers. The cell-control-plane is heavier than your business can support; stay shared-MT with tenant-ID rigour, and migrate when scale forces it.

q3.q: Is that big customer's stack legitimately different (different version, custom integrations, contractual SLO that the shared stack can't meet)?
q3.qhelp: “Big customer” alone doesn't justify a different model — many big customers are happy on shared multi-tenant. The question is whether the big customer's technical requirements diverge.

opts.label: No — same product, just more of it.
opts.body: The customer is big but on the same product, same features, same version, same integrations.

leaf.title: Cell-based. Put the big customer in a dedicated cell; keep everyone else in shared cells.
leaf.verdict: Cell-based architecture lets you isolate the big tenant's blast-radius and capacity without going single-tenant. One large cell sized for the big customer (could be one tenant per cell at this size); 1–3 shared cells for everyone else. Same code, same deploy pipeline, different routing. The big customer gets noisy-neighbour-free operation + dedicated scaling, you keep one deployment story.
when_to_pick: Big customer's load justifies isolation but not a custom stack.
You want to preserve a single product/feature rollout path.
You have the platform team to operate a fleet of cells (even just 2–5).

pros: Blast-radius isolation without per-customer engineering.
Single feature rollout path (all cells run same code).
Big customer gets the SLO they need without contractual heroics.
Add cells as you grow.
cons: Control-plane investment is real (placement, routing, fleet config).
Per-cell idle cost.
Multi-cell observability needs investment.

watch_outs: Avoid the cell-as-a-snowflake trap. The big-customer cell should be the same code as everyone else's, just sized differently.
Negotiate cell-rollout into the SLA. Big customer gets new features 1 sprint later? That's an acceptable trade for blast-radius isolation.
leaf.when_not_to_pick: the big customer is contractually demanding a separate stack with separate version, separate integrations. Then go single-tenant for them.

next_steps.title: AWS Builder's Library — cell-based
next_steps.body: The pattern.

opts.label: Yes — truly bespoke needs.
opts.body: Custom integrations, version pinning, contractual SLO/SLA that the shared stack can't meet, regulator-required deployment shape.

leaf.title: Single-tenant for that customer. Cell-based for the rest. Don't pretend the bespoke stack is the same product.
leaf.verdict: When a customer's needs are genuinely bespoke, run a single-tenant stack for them and a cell-based architecture for everyone else. Critically: do not let the bespoke stack become the trunk — the bespoke fork drifts and eventually you're maintaining two products with one team. Make the bespoke stack pull from main; never the other way. Price the bespoke stack to cover the engineering overhead it creates (typically 1.5–3x base ARR; sometimes 5x+).
when_to_pick: One (or a few) customers contractually require a bespoke deployment shape.
Revenue from those customers justifies a dedicated platform investment.
Your sales motion is enterprise-led, not product-led.

pros: Lets you win the contract.
Bespoke needs don't pollute the main product.
Per-customer SLAs are independently achievable.
cons: Maintenance compounds linearly with #single-tenant customers.
Feature parity drift between bespoke fork and main is a constant tax.
Operationally expensive: one production environment per customer.
Cultural risk: bespoke customer becomes the loudest voice in roadmap.

watch_outs: Encode the rule: bespoke pulls from main; main never pulls from bespoke. The moment that rule breaks, the two products start drifting.
Cap the number of single-tenant customers. Past ~5–10 (depending on team size), the maintenance burden eats more than the revenue.
Price for the overhead. Free single-tenant deployments are a path to bankruptcy.
leaf.when_not_to_pick: you don't have a platform team large enough to operate a fleet of stacks. Then renegotiate the customer back onto cell-based.

next_steps.title: Paved Path Without Adoption
next_steps.body: Same dynamic at the platform layer.

q4.q: How many tenants are on the heterogeneous “head”?
q4.qhelp: Heterogeneous tenancy is the most common SaaS shape: a long tail of small tenants on shared, a head of large enterprise tenants with distinct needs. The number on the head is the variable.

opts.label: 1–3 head tenants.
opts.body: A small number of large enterprises with distinct requirements.

leaf.title: Shared MT for the tail + single-tenant for the head. Plan for cells when head >3.
leaf.verdict: For 1–3 head tenants, the operational simplicity of shared-MT + single-tenant-per-head is fine. Keep main on shared multi-tenant; spin up a single-tenant stack per head tenant where needed. As soon as the head grows to 4+, plan the migration to cell-based — the single-tenant operational tax scales linearly with customer count.
when_to_pick: Long tail of small tenants + 1–3 enterprise heads.
Head tenants justify dedicated stacks contractually.
Platform team is small (cells would be too much investment for the current scale).

pros: Operational simplicity: shared-MT for 95% of customers; bespoke for 1–3.
Each head customer gets full isolation.
No control-plane investment yet.
cons: Doesn't scale past ~3 head customers.
Per-head-stack feature drift if you're not disciplined.

watch_outs: Migrate to cells before the 4th head tenant. Reactive migration is much harder than proactive.
Same fork-discipline as the bespoke case: head stacks pull from main; main never pulls from head.
leaf.when_not_to_pick: the head is already 4+, or growth-rate forecasts that within 12 months. Skip to cells.

next_steps.title: AWS Builder's Library — cells
next_steps.body: Pre-read for the eventual migration.

opts.label: 4 or more head tenants — or growing fast.
opts.body: A meaningful head of enterprise tenants with distinct needs and the count is growing.

leaf.title: Cell-based. Heterogeneity is the natural fit for cells.
leaf.verdict: Cell-based architecture is the natural shape for heterogeneous tenancy at scale. Place each head tenant in its own cell (or pair); shard the tail across shared cells; tenant-placement is your isolation-policy lever. Invest in the control plane: routing, placement, fleet config, schema-migration tooling, multi-cell observability. This is the model major SaaS vendors converge to (Slack, Notion, Linear, Snowflake all run cells).
when_to_pick: 4+ enterprise heads with distinct posture / SLA / residency / version needs.
Long-tail of smaller tenants you want to serve at low unit cost.
Platform team funded for control-plane work.

pros: Per-cell blast-radius, capacity, rollout.
Tenant-placement engine is the policy lever for residency / isolation / SLA.
Scales sub-linearly: adding a 10th cell isn't 10x the work of the first.
cons: Control-plane is a real platform investment (1.5–3+ FTE steady-state).
Per-cell idle cost.
Multi-cell observability + migrations need real tooling.

watch_outs: Build the control plane and migration tooling before shipping the second cell. Don't shard manually — you'll regret it at cell #5.
Standardise cell ops: same Terraform, same dashboards, same alerts. Snowflake cells are the failure mode.
leaf.when_not_to_pick: team is <5 engineers total. Cells will starve the rest of product delivery.

q1.q: How many services / workloads will run on this platform in 12 months?
q1.qhelp: Compute-platform choice is dominated by operational economics, not technology preference. The right answer at 5 services is wrong at 50, and vice versa. The three credible shapes today: managed PaaS (Vercel, Render, Fly.io, App Runner, Container Apps), managed Kubernetes (EKS / GKE / AKS), FaaS (Lambda / Cloud Run / Functions).

opts.label: 1–10 services / workloads.
opts.body: Small product surface; small team; rare service additions.

opts.label: 10–50 services.
opts.body: Mid-sized product surface; established team; regular new-service additions.

opts.label: 50+ services / workloads.
opts.body: Large org or platform-style company; many teams shipping services.

q2_small.q: Is your traffic spiky or steady-state?
q2_small.qhelp: At small scale, the question between PaaS and FaaS comes down to traffic shape and operational preference.

opts.label: Spiky — bursty traffic or scheduled jobs.
opts.body: Variable load; long idle windows; rare batch processing.

leaf.title: FaaS (Lambda / Cloud Run / Functions). Don't stand up Kubernetes.
leaf.verdict: For spiky, low-volume workloads, FaaS is the right shape. Pay-per-invocation amortises idle to zero; the operational surface is just the function code + IAM + monitoring. Avoid Kubernetes — the control-plane and node operational tax for 1–10 services is wildly disproportionate. Pick Cloud Run / AWS Lambda / Azure Functions based on your cloud, not on FaaS framework preference.
when_to_pick: Spiky / bursty traffic with long idle.
Small team that wants to avoid cluster ops.
Stateless workloads (or state in managed services).
Latency-tolerant for cold-start (or use provisioned-concurrency for the hot endpoints).

pros: Zero idle cost on most providers.
Operational simplicity: code + IAM + monitoring.
Auto-scales to zero and back.
Pay-per-request economics align with revenue.
cons: Cold-start latency on first invocation.
Function-runtime + execution-time limits (15 min on Lambda).
Vendor lock-in shape (event sources, deployment shape).
Per-invocation cost can be expensive at very high volume.

watch_outs: Stay stateless or push state to managed services (DynamoDB / RDS / Firestore).
Use provisioned concurrency only for hot, latency-sensitive paths. Otherwise you're paying for idle.
Monitor function cold-start vs warm distribution; mismatched timeout settings here cause “mysterious” outages.
leaf.when_not_to_pick: the workload is long-running (>15 min Lambda, >60 min Cloud Run), latency-sensitive on cold, or stateful in a way that requires persistent local context.

next_steps.title: Service communication
next_steps.body: Sync vs async vs event-driven sits naturally on top of FaaS.

opts.label: Steady — consistent load, hours-on workloads.
opts.body: Web apps, background workers running all the time, predictable traffic.

leaf.title: Managed PaaS (Render / Fly.io / Vercel / App Runner / Container Apps).
leaf.verdict: For steady-state, small-service workloads, managed PaaS is the cost+ops sweet spot. The operational surface is git push → deploy; scaling is configured, not engineered; observability is built-in. Pick based on stack and region: Vercel (Next.js / frontend-heavy), Render (general containers + Postgres bundles), Fly.io (global low-latency, full-stack), AWS App Runner (in-AWS), Azure Container Apps (in-Azure). Re-evaluate when you cross ~10 services or need primitives only K8s offers.
when_to_pick: Steady-state traffic, 1–10 services.
Team is <10 engineers, no dedicated platform person.
Standard stack (containers + Postgres + Redis); no esoteric runtime needs.

pros: Lowest operational overhead of any non-FaaS option.
Built-in: HTTPS, deploy pipeline, observability, secrets.
Faster time-to-prod than K8s for typical apps.
cons: Cost-per-resource is higher than raw EC2 / GCE.
Limited primitives compared to K8s (CronJobs, StatefulSets, custom controllers).
Vendor-shape lock-in (procfile, build pipeline, networking model).
Less flexible for unusual workloads (long-running batch, GPU, custom runtimes).

watch_outs: Validate the cost trajectory. PaaS economics are great at small scale; can flip at mid-scale.
Keep workloads container-portable. When you migrate off PaaS, a Dockerfile + standard env-var config moves cleanly.
Don't lean on platform-specific features unless necessary (e.g. Vercel's edge functions, Render's preview environments). Each one deepens lock-in.
leaf.when_not_to_pick: you anticipate crossing 10 services within a year and want a unified deployment story, or workloads are GPU-bound / require custom runtimes / need K8s primitives.

q2_mid.q: Do you have a dedicated platform team (3+ engineers)?
q2_mid.qhelp: At 10–50 services, the K8s vs PaaS conversation depends almost entirely on whether you have the platform team to operate K8s well.

opts.label: Yes — dedicated platform team.
opts.body: 3+ engineers focused on the developer/operational platform.

leaf.title: Managed Kubernetes (EKS / GKE / AKS). Standardise the substrate.
leaf.verdict: At 10–50 services with a platform team, managed Kubernetes is the right substrate. The operational economics flip in K8s's favour at this scale: shared cluster resources, standard tooling across all services, paved-path scaffolds, one observability stack, one secrets model, one policy engine (see policy engine decision). Pair with a developer portal (Backstage, Cortex, Port) and golden-path templates. Avoid running the K8s control plane yourselves; the managed offerings are good enough.
when_to_pick: 10–50 services, multiple teams, platform-team funded.
Mixed workloads (web, batch, streaming, ML inference).
Multi-tenancy at the platform level (namespace-per-team or cluster-per-environment).

pros: Single substrate across all services.
Operational economy of scale.
Massive ecosystem (operators, controllers, helm charts).
Portable: same workloads run on EKS, GKE, AKS, on-prem K8s.
cons: Cognitive load on developers (without paved paths).
Platform-team headcount is the floor.
Cluster lifecycle (versions, upgrades, node-pool ops) is real work.
Cost overruns from over-provisioned requests/limits.

watch_outs: Build paved paths before opening the cluster to teams. Without templates + golden defaults, K8s becomes the cognitive-load problem it was meant to solve.
Standardise observability + ownership annotations as inherited defaults (not per-team responsibility).
Plan upgrade cadence. Quarterly minor upgrades; budget a 1-day window per cluster per upgrade.
Watch resource-request inflation: most clusters run at ~30% utilisation because requests are over-set. Kubecost / OpenCost visibility helps.
leaf.when_not_to_pick: the platform team doesn't have K8s experience yet. Pay the learning curve in a controlled scope (one team, one cluster, paved-path for one workload type) before opening it up.

opts.label: No — no dedicated platform team.
opts.body: Feature teams are autonomous; ops is shared. No funded platform investment.

leaf.title: Managed PaaS or container-services. Don't adopt K8s without the team to operate it.
leaf.verdict: K8s without a platform team becomes K8s-as-a-tax: every feature team ends up doing operational work badly, in slightly different ways. Stay on managed PaaS (App Runner / Container Apps / Cloud Run for containers + native managed databases) until you fund a platform team. The pattern of adopting K8s “to attract good engineers” or “to be cloud-native” without the team to operate it is a well-documented anti-pattern.
when_to_pick: 10–50 services but no platform team funded.
Feature teams want to own deploys; managed PaaS gives them that.
You'd rather not pay the K8s operational tax.

pros: No platform-team requirement.
Each team can adopt independently.
Operational ceiling is the platform vendor's, not yours.
cons: Different teams may pick different PaaS — observability + security become harder.
Cost-per-service is higher than K8s at this scale.
Migration to K8s later is a real project; the longer you wait, the bigger it is.

watch_outs: Standardise on one PaaS if at all possible. Multi-PaaS becomes the cognitive-load problem.
Track when PaaS cost crosses the platform-team-headcount break-even. That's when you fund the team.
leaf.when_not_to_pick: you can fund a 3+ engineer platform team in the next quarter. Just start with K8s and the paved-path investment.

q2_large.q: Are you running multi-region, multi-cloud, or heavily heterogeneous workloads?
q2_large.qhelp: At 50+ services, the question is no longer K8s-or-not (yes, K8s); it's the shape of the K8s estate.

opts.label: Yes — multi-region / multi-cloud / heterogeneous.
opts.body: Multiple regions for residency or latency; multiple clouds for sovereignty or redundancy; mix of CPU / GPU / batch / streaming workloads.

leaf.title: Managed K8s + multi-cluster control plane. Treat clusters as cattle.
leaf.verdict: At 50+ services across regions/clouds, the K8s estate is itself a platform. Don't run one giant cluster; run many small clusters (per region, per environment, per blast-radius zone) and operate them via a multi-cluster control plane (ArgoCD / Flux ApplicationSets, Cluster API, Karmada, or commercial: Rancher / Anthos / EKS Anywhere fleet). The platform team's job becomes fleet management: golden cluster templates, policy distribution, observability aggregation, multi-cluster rollouts.
when_to_pick: 50+ services across multiple regions or clouds.
Sovereignty / residency drives separate clusters.
Blast-radius isolation requires multiple clusters per region.

pros: Per-cluster blast radius.
Per-region / per-cloud isolation respects residency without bolt-ons.
Standardised cluster templates compound across the fleet.
cons: Fleet management is a real engineering investment.
Multi-cluster observability + service-mesh adds complexity.
Cost amortisation is worse than a single giant cluster.

watch_outs: Don't let any cluster become a snowflake. Snowflake clusters erase the fleet model.
Policy distribution is the control plane's job (OPA bundle server, Kyverno policies-as-CRDs distributed via GitOps).
Multi-cluster service mesh is hard. Don't adopt mesh-everywhere as the first move; pair traffic patterns to mesh adoption.
leaf.when_not_to_pick: you only need multiple clusters for environments (dev/staging/prod) and they're all in the same region. That's one operational model; not multi-cluster proper.

opts.label: No — single region/cloud, homogeneous workloads.
opts.body: Big org but one cloud, one region (or a few same-region clusters), standard workload shapes.

leaf.title: Managed K8s, one (or a few) production clusters, paved-path-driven.
leaf.verdict: For 50+ services in a single estate, managed K8s + platform-team-owned paved paths is the answer. Run 1 production cluster per blast-radius zone (typically prod / staging / dev) + a tenant-isolation model in production (namespaces + RBAC + network policies). The work is the paved-path layer: scaffolds, golden defaults, observability inheritance, ownership annotations, policy enforcement. The cluster itself should feel boring; the platform on top is the value.
when_to_pick: 50+ services, single region/cloud, homogeneous workloads.
Platform team funded and product-mindset-oriented.
You want a single deployment story across all teams.

pros: Operational simplicity vs multi-cluster.
Best cost amortisation across services.
Single observability + policy + ownership story.
cons: Blast-radius is the cluster.
Capacity events affect all teams.
Migration to multi-cluster later is real work.

watch_outs: Plan the second-cluster pattern from day one. Eventually you'll add another for blast radius or region; templates should support it.
Pod-disruption-budgets + cluster-autoscaler tuning become real engineering at this scale.
leaf.when_not_to_pick: you anticipate multi-region within 12 months. Start with the multi-cluster pattern even if you only have one cluster live.

q1.q: Does the caller need an answer to complete its own work?
q1.qhelp: The fundamental fork in service-to-service communication is whether the caller needs the callee's response synchronously. Get this wrong and you'll either over-engineer with queues (when sync would have worked) or build hidden coupling chains (when async would have decoupled).

opts.label: Yes — the caller needs the result.
opts.body: Authorisation check, pricing lookup, account validation, inventory check — the caller's next step depends on the response.

opts.label: No — the caller just notifies.
opts.body: Order-placed; user-created; payment-completed — many downstream things care, but the caller doesn't need their work to complete its own.

opts.label: Sometimes both — same domain event, multiple consumers, different needs.
opts.body: “User signed up” — auth needs sync confirmation; analytics, email, recommendation, billing can be async.

leaf.title: Sync for the critical path + event for the rest. The shape is “CQRS-lite” at the service boundary.
leaf.verdict: The right answer for mixed-consumer events is: sync API call for the part the caller depends on (e.g. "create user, return user ID") + event publish for everything else ("user.created" event, consumed independently by analytics, email, recs, billing). This avoids both over-coupling (everything sync) and under-confirming (everything async, no caller confirmation). The event-bus is the integration substrate; the API is the contract for the caller's critical path.
when_to_pick: Multiple downstream consumers of the same domain event.
Caller needs confirmation of one slice but not the others.
You want to decouple analytics / notification / billing from the critical path.

pros: Critical path stays fast and confirmed.
Non-critical consumers can fail / be slow without affecting the caller.
New consumers don't change the API contract.
cons: Two paths to operate (sync + event-bus).
Idempotency on both paths matters.
Eventual consistency in the async paths needs to be reflected in product UX.

watch_outs: Idempotency keys on both the sync API and the event consumers. Without them, retries cause duplicates.
Order matters when it matters. If two events on the same entity must be ordered, you need a partitioned event bus (Kafka by key) or a sequencing strategy.
Don't make the event bus the source of truth for the caller's critical-path data. The sync return value is the authoritative record.
leaf.when_not_to_pick: your event bus isn't reliable (no durability, no exactly-once-or-better delivery). Then keep everything sync until the bus is production-grade.

q2_sync.q: Is the call cross-organisation, cross-team, or cross-platform?
q2_sync.qhelp: Sync calls have a protocol choice: REST/HTTP, gRPC, GraphQL. The choice depends largely on who's on each end of the wire.

opts.label: Cross-org or public — external consumers.
opts.body: Partner API, public SDK, mobile/web clients you don't control.

leaf.title: REST + OpenAPI. Don't make external consumers learn your framework.
leaf.verdict: For cross-organisation / public APIs, REST + OpenAPI 3.x is the right default. Every language has good tooling; every developer can read it; OpenAPI gives you contract-driven SDK generation; HTTP semantics work through every proxy/CDN/firewall. gRPC works only if you control both sides; GraphQL works for a narrow set of mobile-app-shaped consumers but adds significant operational complexity for general use. Pair REST with consumer-driven contract tests (Pact) to catch breaking changes.
when_to_pick: Cross-organisation, partner-facing, or public-SDK APIs.
Heterogeneous consumer stack (mobile, web, partner-server, scripts).
You can't push tooling updates to consumers in lockstep.

pros: Universal tooling, debuggable with curl/browser.
OpenAPI generates client SDKs in every language.
Works through every network appliance.
Semantic HTTP (caching, retries, idempotency) is well understood.
cons: Verbose payloads compared to gRPC/Protobuf.
Versioning discipline is on you (URL versioning, semver schemas, deprecation).
REST design is genuinely hard to do well; team conventions matter.

watch_outs: Generate the OpenAPI spec from code (not the other way), or vice versa — pick one and enforce it. Hand-maintaining both is the path to drift.
Contract tests beat integration tests for cross-org APIs. Pact pattern.
Deprecation policy: published, dated, enforced. Without it, removal becomes a political negotiation.
leaf.when_not_to_pick: you absolutely need streaming over the same connection (server-push / bidi). Then gRPC or WebSockets/SSE for the streaming surface.

opts.label: Intra-platform — you control both ends.
opts.body: Internal microservices on your own platform, consistent stack, deploy lockstep possible.

leaf.title: gRPC + Protobuf. Significantly better than REST for internal calls.
leaf.verdict: For internal service-to-service calls where you control both ends, gRPC is materially better than REST: schema-first contracts (Protobuf), strongly-typed clients in every language, smaller payloads, native streaming support, HTTP/2 multiplexing. Add a service mesh (Istio / Linkerd / consul-connect) for mTLS, retries, observability defaults — these matter at intra-platform scale. Use REST at the platform edge (BFF / API gateway); gRPC behind it.
when_to_pick: Internal service-to-service calls.
Multiple languages on the platform (Protobuf is genuinely cross-language).
Streaming or bi-directional flows matter.
You have or can adopt a service mesh.

pros: Strongly-typed contracts; breaking changes show at compile time.
Smaller payloads, faster encoding.
Native streaming + HTTP/2 multiplexing.
Protobuf evolution rules are explicit and well-documented.
cons: Less debuggable than REST (need grpcurl + reflection).
Browsers + most proxies don't speak gRPC natively.
Learning curve for teams new to Protobuf.
Service-mesh complexity if adopted.

watch_outs: Treat .proto files as the source of truth. Stored in a single proto-repo (or per-domain), versioned, compatibility-checked in CI (buf breaking).
Plan a REST/HTTP edge for browser clients. gRPC-Web works but isn't a free lunch.
Don't adopt service-mesh as the first move. Start without mesh; add when latency/observability/security gaps justify it.
leaf.when_not_to_pick: your platform is heterogeneous and you can't deploy clients in lockstep (e.g. third-party plugins). REST is more forgiving.

q2_async.q: Do you need ordering, replay, or many independent consumers?
q2_async.qhelp: Async messaging splits into queue (one consumer per message; no ordering / replay) vs event log / stream (many consumers; ordered; replayable). The choice depends on what you'll do with the events later.

opts.label: Queue — one consumer, work distribution.
opts.body: Background jobs, send email, process upload. One consumer pulls; competing consumers OK for throughput.

leaf.title: Managed queue (SQS / Cloud Tasks / Service Bus / RabbitMQ).
leaf.verdict: For work-distribution patterns (one logical consumer per message), pick the managed queue native to your cloud: AWS SQS, GCP Cloud Tasks, Azure Service Bus. Operational simplicity, durable, scales sub-linearly with cost. Skip Kafka here — you don't need its features and you'll pay its operational tax. RabbitMQ is fine if you need richer routing patterns (topic exchanges, fanout) without committing to a streaming platform.
when_to_pick: Work distribution: produce-once, consume-once.
Don't need replay, ordering, or many consumers.
Want operational simplicity.

pros: Operationally minimal (managed).
Cheap.
Right primitive for the job.
cons: No replay (you can't reprocess yesterday's messages).
Generally not ordered (FIFO queues exist but at lower throughput).
Pivoting to event-streaming later is real work.

watch_outs: Always set dead-letter queues + alarms on DLQ depth. Silent failures otherwise.
Idempotent consumers. At-least-once delivery is the default; design for it.
Visibility timeouts tuned to the work, not the default.
leaf.when_not_to_pick: you anticipate adding multiple independent consumers of the same events later. Pick an event-streaming primitive from the start; queue-to-stream migration is expensive.

opts.label: Event stream — many consumers, ordered, replayable.
opts.body: Domain events: "order.placed" consumed by ten different downstream systems. Need replay for new consumers / backfills.

leaf.title: Kafka (or managed: MSK / Confluent Cloud / Redpanda / Azure Event Hubs).
leaf.verdict: For multi-consumer ordered replayable event streams, Kafka (or a Kafka-compatible managed service) is the industry default. Partitioning gives you ordered-per-key semantics; retention gives you replay; consumer groups give you many independent consumers. Use managed (MSK / Confluent / Aiven / Redpanda Cloud) unless you have a dedicated streaming-platform team; self-managed Kafka is a real operational commitment. Azure Event Hubs is a viable Kafka-protocol alternative in Azure-native estates.
when_to_pick: Many independent consumers of the same events.
Need replay (new consumer joins → consumes from offset N or beginning).
Ordering per-entity matters.
Stream-processing on the events (KSQL, Flink, Beam) is on the roadmap.

pros: Right primitive for many-consumer event flow.
Replay enables new consumers to backfill from history.
Partitioning gives ordered-per-key semantics at scale.
Ecosystem: Kafka Connect, Streams, KSQL, Schema Registry.
cons: Operational footprint is real even when managed (partition planning, consumer-group management, schema evolution).
Cost at scale is material.
Over-engineering risk: many orgs adopt Kafka before they need it.

watch_outs: Schema Registry (Avro / Protobuf) is non-optional for any non-trivial event flow.
Partition key choice is the single most important schema decision. Changing it later requires re-keying.
Plan consumer-lag monitoring + alerts. Lag = a consumer is falling behind or stuck; silent.
Don't over-partition early. Adding partitions to a topic is operationally awkward; start conservatively.
leaf.when_not_to_pick: your event volume is <100K events/day and there are 1–2 consumers. Use a queue.

q1.q: How many engineers are working in this codebase today?
q1.qhelp: The strongest predictor of the right decomposition is team size + coordination overhead, not technology fit. Microservices were popularised because Conway's Law made coordination across large orgs intolerable — not because they made the software better. Pick based on how many people need to ship independently.

opts.label: 1–10 engineers.
opts.body: Single team or two small teams. Everyone can read every change in standup.

leaf.title: Monolith. Not as a compromise — as the right answer.
leaf.verdict: A monolith for 1–10 engineers is not a stop-gap; it's the right answer. One codebase, one deploy, one process, one observability stack. The microservices tax (separate deploys, network calls, distributed tracing, service-mesh, etc.) costs more than the coordination it saves at this scale. If you've adopted microservices at 1–10 engineers, you're paying the wrong tax. Re-evaluate at 10+ engineers or when one team is consistently blocked by another's deploy cadence.
when_to_pick: 1–10 engineers.
Single team or 2 small teams.
Product is still finding shape; refactoring within a monolith is faster than across services.

pros: One codebase to navigate, refactor, test.
One deploy pipeline.
Cheapest operationally.
Refactoring is local, not distributed.
No network-call failure modes between modules.
cons: Single deploy: a bug in one feature blocks all deploys.
Single scale unit: can't scale features independently.
Team coordination overhead grows past ~10.

watch_outs: Even monoliths need module boundaries. Keep concerns separated in code (package-per-domain), even if you deploy as one.
Don't bake in global mutable state. The monolith-to-modular-monolith migration is easy; monolith-with-globals to anything is hard.
Pick a framework you can grow with (Rails / Django / Phoenix / Spring / Laravel / Next.js full-stack) — not one optimised for tiny apps.
leaf.when_not_to_pick: you're at 10+ engineers already — you're already past this decision point.

opts.label: 10–50 engineers.
opts.body: Multiple teams; coordination overhead is starting to be felt; deploy cadence is contested.

opts.label: 50+ engineers.
opts.body: Large organisation; many teams; cross-team coordination is its own problem.

leaf.title: Microservices, organised by Team Topologies shapes.
leaf.verdict: At 50+ engineers, microservices stop being optional. The cost of cross-team coordination in a single codebase outweighs the cost of distributed-systems complexity. Critical: decompose by team and bounded context, not by technical layer. Use Team Topologies shapes — stream-aligned teams own end-to-end services; enabling teams cross-pollinate; platform teams own the substrate. Skipping this and decomposing by technical layer (UI service, business-logic service, data service) recreates the monolith problem with network hops.
when_to_pick: 50+ engineers, multiple teams.
Multiple business lines / product areas.
Platform team funded; service mesh / observability substrate in place.

pros: Independent deploys; teams move at their own pace.
Independent scaling per service.
Team ownership is clear.
Failures are local-by-default (if designed right).
cons: Distributed-systems complexity (consistency, partial failure, tracing).
Operational footprint multiplies with service count.
Need real platform substrate (deploy, observability, mesh, secrets, IDP).
Wrong boundaries = network-call hell.

watch_outs: Boundaries follow team / bounded context, never layer. If a service exists because “the UI team made it,” it'll always be coupled to one other service.
Plan distributed-tracing + centralised logs from day one.
Service ownership annotations are required, not optional. Anonymous services rot.
Watch out for the distributed monolith: services that can't deploy independently because every change touches three of them. That's coupling pretending to be decoupling.
leaf.when_not_to_pick: you're decomposing for technology reasons ("to use Go" / "to be cloud-native") rather than team reasons. Restart from the team-boundary lens.

q2_mid.q: Are teams genuinely blocked by each other's deploy cadence or coordination overhead?
q2_mid.qhelp: “Microservices would let us move faster” is often aspirational at this scale. The diagnostic question is whether the blocking is real or imagined.

opts.label: No — coordination works fine.
opts.body: Teams can deploy on their own cadence inside the monolith. Coordination overhead is manageable.

leaf.title: Modular monolith. Get the team-boundary benefits without the network-call tax.
leaf.verdict: The modular monolith is the under-rated middle ground for 10–50 engineers when coordination isn't broken yet. One deploy unit, but enforced module boundaries (package-per-domain, dependency rules, internal APIs between modules). Teams own modules; deploys are shared but predictable. Refactoring across module boundaries is easier than across services. This is the shape that big-monolith success stories (Shopify, GitHub, Basecamp, Stack Overflow at various points) actually run.
when_to_pick: 10–50 engineers, multiple teams, but deploy cadence isn't a fight yet.
Product is still evolving; bounded contexts are not yet stable.
You want the team-ownership clarity of services without the distributed-systems tax.

pros: Module ownership without service operational tax.
Refactoring across modules is local, not distributed.
Single deploy story; single observability stack.
Pivots between bounded contexts are cheap.
cons: Module boundary discipline must be enforced (in code, in CI).
Coupled deploys: a release-blocker in one module blocks others.
Scale unit is still global.
Migration to microservices later is a real project (but easier from a modular monolith than from a tangled one).

watch_outs: Enforce module boundaries in CI. Compile-time / package-level dependency rules. Without enforcement, modules become friends-with-benefits.
Internal APIs between modules should be treated like real APIs. Versioned; tested; deprecated cleanly.

Quarterly review: are any modules ready to graduate to services? The right time to extract a service is when team ownership is stable, the module has a high deploy contention rate, and its dependencies on the rest are minimal.
leaf.when_not_to_pick: team coordination is genuinely broken — teams routinely block each other on releases. Then extract the contended modules to services.

opts.label: Yes — teams routinely block each other.
opts.body: Deploy queues; merge contention; release-trains that nobody likes. Coordination overhead is felt every sprint.

leaf.title: Selective extraction to services — not big-bang microservices.
leaf.verdict: The wrong move here is the big-bang microservices migration; the right move is selective extraction. Identify the modules with the highest deploy-contention (where teams routinely wait on each other), the most stable bounded contexts (won't be re-shaped in 6 months), and the fewest cross-module dependencies. Extract those first; leave the rest in the monolith. The monolith stays the centre of gravity for product-finding work; extracted services exist where independence is paid for in operational tax willingly. Plan to grow the extracted-service count over 2–4 quarters, not overnight.
when_to_pick: 10–50 engineers, real deploy-coordination pain.
Some bounded contexts are stable and could move independently.
Platform team funded (or being funded) to operate the extracted services.

pros: Solves the actual problem (specific teams blocking each other) without buying the full microservices tax.
Extraction is incremental, reversible.
Monolith stays as the playground for new bounded contexts.
cons: Two operational worlds (monolith + N services).
Need data-ownership clarity at every extraction.
Cross-monolith-and-service queries become coordination work.

watch_outs: Strangler-fig pattern: extract by routing traffic, not by big-bang rewrite. Martin Fowler's original post.
Data ownership moves with the service. If the extracted service still queries the monolith's database, it's not extracted; it's a distributed coupling.
Don't extract for the sake of extraction. Each extraction must close a specific coordination pain — otherwise you're paying operational tax for nothing.
leaf.when_not_to_pick: you're at 50+ engineers — go straight to the microservices recommendation; selective extraction is too slow at that scale.
